Q: Comparison of dates and coloring text in vuejs A:

Try this. <p :class=" date1 > currentDate ? 'abc text-red' : 'abc'">{{ date1 }}. And create a new variable called currentDate and set it to new Date() in the created() hook. This adds the class text-red when date1 > currentDate is true

Q: How to calculate distance or error line in an image? A:

Here is one approach in Python OpenCV.

  • Read the input image and get its dimensions. This removes the alpha channel.

  • Crop the input to remove the thin white border around the bounds of the image

  • Threshold on the white box

  • Apply morphology to close gaps

  • Get the largest contour

  • Reduce the contour to 4 points, i.e. a rectangle

  • Draw the polygon in green on a copy of the input

  • Threshold the image for the red curve

  • Get the largest contour and its number of points

  • Loop over this contour: Do a point in polygon test for each point in the contour agains the polygon to get its distance from the point to the polygon. Accumulate the sum of the distances.

  • Compute the average distance and print it

  • Save the images

Input image with transparency:

import cv2
import numpy as np

# read the input image (removes the alpha channel)
img = cv2.imread('red_curve.png')
hh, ww = img.shape[:2]

# remove outer white border
img = img[2:hh-2, 2:ww-2]

# threshold on the white rectangle
low = (150,150,150)
high = (255,255,255)
thresh1 = cv2.inRange(img, low, high)

# apply morphology close to fill in gaps
kernel = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_RECT, (25,25))
morph1 = cv2.morphologyEx(thresh1, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, kernel)
kernel = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_CROSS, (11,11))
morph1 = cv2.morphologyEx(morph1, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, kernel)

# get largest contour
contours = cv2.findContours(morph1, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
contours = contours[0] if len(contours) == 2 else contours[1]
big_contour1 = max(contours, key=cv2.contourArea)
#print(len(big_contour))

# reduce to a rectangle
peri = cv2.arcLength(big_contour1, True)
polygon = cv2.approxPolyDP(big_contour1, 0.01 * peri, True)
#print(len(polygon))

# draw polygon on a copy of the input
poly_img = img.copy()
cv2.polylines(poly_img, [polygon], True, (0,255,0), 1)

# thresh the image for the red curve
low = (0,0,255)
high = (0,0,255)
thresh2 = cv2.inRange(img, low, high)

# get largest contour
contours = cv2.findContours(thresh2, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
contours = contours[0] if len(contours) == 2 else contours[1]
big_contour2 = max(contours, key=cv2.contourArea)
num_pts = len(big_contour2)

# do point in polygon to get distances between points on red contour 
# to points on rectangle
sum_distances = 0
for pt in big_contour2:
    x = float(pt[0][0])
    y = float(pt[0][1])
    dist = cv2.pointPolygonTest(polygon, (x, y), True)
    sum_distances = sum_distances + abs(dist)
average_distance = sum_distances / num_pts

# print average distance
print(f"Average Distance: {average_distance:>0.02f}")

# save images
cv2.imwrite('red_curve_crop.png', img)
cv2.imwrite('red_curve_thresh1.png', thresh1)
cv2.imwrite('red_curve_morph1.png', morph1)
cv2.imwrite('red_curve_polygon.png', poly_img)
cv2.imwrite('red_curve_thresh2.png', thresh2)

# show results
cv2.imshow('cropped image', img)
cv2.imshow('thresh1', thresh1)
cv2.imshow('morph1', morph1)
cv2.imshow('polygon', poly_img)
cv2.imshow('thresh2', thresh2)
cv2.waitKey(0)
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

Q: jqueryvalidation.org cert errors A:

This appears to be a problem with the website's SSL certificate, not with the jQuery Validation Plugin itself.

The current release is 1.22.1, and it is available through npm:

npm install jquery-validation

You can also download the release from the project's GitHub repository.

The Link

So if jqueryvalidation.org is showing an invalid certificate, you don't need to bypass the browser warning; use the official repository/npm package instead.

Q: Canonical way to select data in SQLAlchemy A:

For SQLAlchemy 2.x, prefer the 2.0-style select() API:

stmt = select(MyTable).where(
    MyTable.column1 == value1,
    MyTable.column2 == value2
)
rows = session.scalars(stmt).all()

session.query() is the legacy API retained mainly for compatibility with older code. filter() and filter_by() are still available, but they are methods on that legacy Query interface.

Use filter_by() when you simply have keyword equality filters:

select(MyTable).filter_by(column1=value1, column2=value2)

For anything more expressive, where() with SQL expressions is generally clearer.

So for new SQLAlchemy 2.x code: select() + where()/filter_by() + session.scalars().

Q: How can I determine if a phone number is WhatsApp-enabled before sending a message using WhatsApp Cloud API? A:

There's no official pre-check in the Cloud API. The On-Premises API had a /contacts endpoint that did exactly this, and Meta dropped it from Cloud. Anything that claims to check a number without sending is either scraping the consumer app or guessing.

What you actually get is the answer after the fact, through the statuses webhook:

  • sent means the number exists on WhatsApp and Meta accepted the message for that account. This is the signal you want. It arrives within a second or two, before delivered.
  • delivered means it reached a device. A number can sit at sent for days if the phone is off, so don't treat "not delivered" as "not on WhatsApp".
  • failed with error code 131026 (message undeliverable) is the closest thing to "not a WhatsApp number". It's not exact. The same code comes back when the recipient hasn't accepted the current terms of service, or has blocked your business number, or the number is on WhatsApp but only via the older versions that can't receive template messages.

So the practical design is the one you already described, with two tweaks:

  1. Store the result per number with a timestamp, not just a boolean. whatsapp_status, whatsapp_checked_at. People change numbers and uninstall, so age it out. 30 to 90 days is a normal choice.
  2. Set the flag on sent, not on delivered, and clear it on 131026. A successful OTP verification is the strongest positive signal you'll ever have, so if the number has passed an OTP over WhatsApp you can trust it longer than a plain sent.

For the very first message to an unknown number, you have to send something to find out. A template message is the only kind you can send outside the 24 hour window anyway, so the first OTP or first notification doubles as the probe. Keep an SMS fallback behind the 131026 path so the first message still reaches the person.

Disclosure, since it's relevant: I work at MyOTP.App, an OTP delivery service. 131026 is the bucket we track separately as "bad number" on our own WhatsApp sends, and it's noisy for exactly the reasons above. The logic here is the same whether you build it on the Cloud API yourself or use a vendor.
